title: UTI Management - Cystitis in a Man
patient_instructions: You are Gary Fletcher, a 52-year-old man who has had burning when passing urine, needing to go more often, and some lower tummy discomfort for 3 days. You noticed a small amount of pink/blood-tinged urine yesterday, which frightened you. No fever or shakes, no loin/back pain, no nausea (so nothing to suggest the infection has gone to the kidneys). No difficulty starting the stream or dribbling before this, no penile discharge. You are a smoker (20/day for 30 years). You are penicillin allergic (you got a rash as a child). No other medications. Your urine dipstick in the clinic showed leucocytes and nitrites, and a sample has been sent for culture. Your IDEAS: you think it is 'just a water infection'. Your CONCERNS: you are worried the blood in the urine means cancer. Your EXPECTATIONS: you want antibiotics and to be told the blood is nothing serious. Affect: cooperative, keen for reassurance about the blood. Ask the doctor directly: 'Does the blood mean I have cancer?'
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Gary Fletcher, 52, a smoker, presents with 3 days of dysuria, frequency and one episode of blood-stained urine; dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites and an MSU has been sent. Tasks: explain the likely diagnosis and its management, choose an appropriate antibiotic, and address his concern about the blood in his urine. You do not need to take a full history. The examiner is looking for correct Australian antibiotic selection accounting for penicillin allergy, appropriate treatment duration for a male UTI, and crucially a safe plan for follow-up of haematuria rather than false reassurance.
examiner_instructions: The candidate should diagnose lower UTI (cystitis) in a man - noting UTI is uncommon in men so a first episode warrants thought about structural/prostatic causes. Correct Australian antibiotic choice: first-line trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 7 days in a man (penicillin allergy does not affect trimethoprim); alternatives nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release BD (contraindicated if eGFR <45 and must NOT be used if prostatitis/pyelonephritis suspected) or cephalexin. Paracetamol is first-line analgesia; Ural (alkaliniser) gives symptomatic relief. CRITICAL teaching point: haematuria in an adult man (especially a smoker over 40) must NOT be dismissed as 'just the UTI' - recheck urine after treatment and, if it persists, refer for urine cytology, CT urography and cystoscopy to exclude urothelial/bladder cancer. If prostatitis is present, treat 14-28 days with an agent that penetrates the prostate (trimethoprim or fluoroquinolone), not a flat 14 days. Note Hiprex is a prophylactic urinary antiseptic requiring acidic urine, NOT an analgesic alkaliniser, and must not be co-prescribed with Ural. Use the rubric.

criteria: Confirms cystitis symptoms and excludes upper-tract/systemic features (fever, loin pain)
Screens for prostatic/obstructive symptoms and risk factors (smoking, age)
Notes MSU sent for culture and interprets dipstick
Identifies penicillin allergy and checks renal function relevance
Diagnoses lower UTI (cystitis) in a man and recognises UTI in men is uncommon/complicated
Recognises haematuria requires its own evaluation and does not attribute it solely to UTI
Correct antibiotic: trimethoprim 300 mg daily 7 days (allergy-appropriate); paracetamol analgesia; symptomatic Ural
Plan to recheck urine post-treatment and refer for cytology/CT urography/cystoscopy if haematuria persists; longer course (14-28 days) if prostatitis
Explains diagnosis and honest haematuria follow-up plan without false reassurance; explores ICE

red_flags: Persistent visible or non-visible haematuria in a man over 40 or a smoker - investigate for urothelial/bladder malignancy
Fever, rigors, loin pain or systemic upset - pyelonephritis or prostatitis rather than simple cystitis
Recurrent UTI in a man - structural or prostatic pathology requiring urology referral
Failure of symptoms to resolve after appropriate antibiotics - reassess and image the urinary tract
australian_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines (Antibiotic): male cystitis - trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 7 days first-line; alternatives nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release BD (avoid if eGFR <45 or prostatitis/pyelonephritis suspected) or cephalexin; acute bacterial prostatitis 14-28 days with a prostate-penetrating agent
RACGP / Cancer Council: haematuria in an adult (especially smoker >40) requires urine cytology, CT urography and cystoscopy to exclude urothelial cancer; recheck urine after treatment
Antimicrobial stewardship and PBS-listed agents; paracetamol first-line analgesia with cautious NSAID use given nephrotoxicity risk in infection/dehydration
learning_objectives: Select guideline-concordant antibiotics for male cystitis accounting for allergy and renal function
Recognise UTI in men as complicated and consider prostatic/structural causes
Investigate haematuria appropriately rather than attributing it to UTI
Communicate a safe follow-up and safety-netting plan
key_points: Penicillin allergy does not affect trimethoprim, the first-line agent for male cystitis
Do not attribute haematuria in an adult man to UTI - recheck and investigate to exclude bladder cancer
Hiprex is prophylaxis requiring acidic urine and must not be combined with Ural (an alkaliniser)
Acute bacterial prostatitis needs 14-28 days of a prostate-penetrating antibiotic

citations.claim: Haematuria must not be dismissed - painless frank haematuria (especially in an at-risk adult) is an ominous sign indicating possible malignancy, supporting follow-up of UTI-attributed haematuria.

The management phase of the consultation (explanation/education, prescribing, follow-up and safety-netting) frames how this station's diagnosis, investigation and red-flag advice should be structured.
